_about: DRAFT for Nav's approval (phase 7b). The six milestones on the route, in km travelled from Earth. Each fact was checked against the NASA/JPL pages in 'sources' on 2026-11-19 (Product principle 5). 'fact' and 'sub' show in the milestone moment (1e) and the log; 'page' is the fact page at /milestones/<slug>. Milestones 3 and 4 keep the design's names and distances.

milestones.name: Past the Moon
milestones.title: Past the Moon!
milestones.fact: The Moon is on average 384,400 km from Earth. The Apollo crews took about three days to get this far.
milestones.sub: We're not stopping for the view.
milestones.description: Milestone 1 of the OneSmallClick mission: the Moon's orbit, 384,400 km from Earth, and how long the Apollo crews took to get there.
page: The first milestone is the Moon's orbit. On average the Moon is 384,400 km from Earth, but its orbit is not a perfect circle, so the real distance changes through the month.

The Apollo astronauts took about three days to cross this gap. OSC-1 never stops coasting at 21 km a second, so the crew passes the Moon's orbit within about five hours of launch: the first sign that everything is working.

sources.label: NASA Scientific Visualization Studio: Earth-Moon distance

milestones.name: Webb's neighbourhood
milestones.title: Waving at Webb
milestones.fact: The James Webb Space Telescope circles a point called L2, about 1.5 million km from Earth. Webb took about a month to get there.
milestones.sub: Four times as far as the Moon, and still only the start.
milestones.description: Milestone 2 of the OneSmallClick mission: 1.5 million km out, near the L2 point where the James Webb Space Telescope works.
page: About 1.5 million km from Earth, on the side facing away from the Sun, lies the second Lagrange point, L2. A spacecraft near L2 stays in line with Earth as both go round the Sun, so its sunshield can block the Sun, Earth and Moon at once, and its radio link to Earth stays steady.
The James Webb Space Telescope doesn't sit at L2 itself. It loops round the point on a wide halo orbit, once every 168 days. It took Webb about a month to travel out there after launch.

milestones.name: Mid-course burn
milestones.title: Mid-course burn complete
milestones.fact: Radio travels at the speed of light, so a ping across 120 million km takes about 7 minutes to arrive.
milestones.sub: Every Ping you send is already history when it lands.
milestones.description: Milestone 3 of the OneSmallClick mission: 120 million km out, where real Mars probes fine-tune their course and radio signals take minutes to arrive.
page: Real Mars probes don't fly a perfect line. On the way they fire their thrusters a few times to fine-tune the path; these are called trajectory correction manoeuvres. NASA's Perseverance rover planned several during its cruise to Mars in 2020 and 2021, using eight small thrusters on its cruise stage.
Distance starts to show in the radio link, too. Signals travel at about 300,000 km a second, so a message across 120 million km takes about 6 minutes 40 seconds each way.

milestones.name: Halfway
milestones.title: Halfway to Mars!
milestones.fact: Sunlight takes about 8 minutes 20 seconds to cross the 150 million km to Earth. We've now flown farther than that.
milestones.sub: From here on, Mars is closer than home.
milestones.description: Milestone 4 of the OneSmallClick mission: halfway along the 480 million km route, farther than the distance from the Sun to Earth.
page: Halfway along our 480 million km route. From here on, every kilometre the crew pushes brings Mars closer than home.

The average distance from the Sun to Earth, about 150 million km, is called an astronomical unit. Sunlight takes about 8 minutes 20 seconds to cross it, so the Sun you see is always a little in the past. OSC-1 has now travelled farther than that.

sources.label: NASA: Voyager 1, what is a light-day?

milestones.name: Three quarters
milestones.title: Three quarters there
milestones.fact: A day on Mars, called a sol, lasts 24 hours 39 minutes: just a little longer than ours.
milestones.sub: Rover teams on Earth have lived on Mars time to keep up.
milestones.description: Milestone 5 of the OneSmallClick mission: three quarters of the way, and how long a day on Mars really is.
page: Three quarters of the way there, so it's time to get ready for Mars time. A Mars solar day, called a sol, lasts 24 hours 39 minutes 35 seconds on average.
Those extra 40 minutes add up. When NASA's rovers land, their teams on Earth often work on Mars time for the first months, starting each working day about 40 minutes later than the one before.

milestones.name: Phobos in view
milestones.title: Phobos in view
milestones.fact: Phobos orbits only about 6,000 km above Mars, closer to its planet than any other known moon.
milestones.sub: It races round Mars three times a day.
milestones.description: Milestone 6 of the OneSmallClick mission: Phobos, the Mars moon that orbits closer to its planet than any other known moon.
page: Mars has two small moons, Phobos and Deimos. Phobos, the bigger one, orbits only about 6,000 km above the Martian surface: no other known moon orbits so close to its planet. It goes round Mars three times a day.
Phobos is slowly spiralling inwards. Scientists expect it to break apart in 30 to 50 million years. For now it's the first sign that we're nearly there.

sources.label: NASA: Mars' moon Phobos is slowly falling apart
